1261.title: Contemplation to attain love
1261.hook: love shows itself in deeds; take, Lord, receive
1261.howItsDone: The Suscipe closes the Spiritual Exercises' contemplation to attain love; some who pray in the Ignatian way say it at the end of a retreat, and some pray it daily.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth week: the risen Christ as consoler, with a name, a walk, a breakfast on the beach. Your line was the consoler.

After the fourth week, the Exercises turn to a contemplation, and Ignatius opens it with two short remarks before any prayer at all. First: love ought to show itself more in deeds than in words. Second: love is a sharing. The lover gives the beloved what they have, and the beloved gives back. Two sentences, plain as a kitchen table. No grand theory of love. Everything that follows hangs from them, including a short prayer of offering, written right into the text.
screen: `MORE IN DEEDS THAN IN WORDS.` → `LOVE IS A SHARING.` → `THEN, A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The contemplation to attain love asks the person to look back over everything received. Creation. Redemption. The particular gifts of one's own life: the people, the chances, the mercies. Ignatius says to ponder how much God has done, and how God wants to give, as far as possible, God's own self. Then the two remarks come back. If love is a sharing, and God has given this much, what does a person give back? Ignatius answers with a prayer, offered as if by someone moved by great love. It's known by its first Latin word, Suscipe: receive. In substance it goes like this. Take, Lord, receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding, my whole will, everything I have and possess. You gave it to me; I give it back. It's all yours; dispose of it as you will. Give me only your love and your grace; that is enough for me. Look at what is offered: not money, not a list of good works, but freedom, memory, mind and will, the very things the Exercises have been training all along. Indifference, discernment, the choice made from the end. All of it, handed back. And what is asked in return: only love and grace. The First Letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims, makes the same point about deeds: "let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth." So the Suscipe is not meant to stay a sentence.
screen: `LOOK BACK AT WHAT YOU'VE BEEN GIVEN.` · `IF LOVE IS SHARING, WHAT GOES BACK?` · `LIBERTY, MEMORY, UNDERSTANDING, WILL.` · `ONLY LOVE AND GRACE.` · then, large: `IN DEED, AND IN TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open. If you know the Suscipe, pray it slowly, a phrase on each breath; if not, use today's line, take, Lord, receive, and name one at a time what Ignatius offers: my freedom, my memory, my mind, my will. If you don't pray, sit with the question underneath it: what am I holding that I could hand over?
Suscipe. Receive: the first word of Ignatius's prayer of offering, which hands back freedom, memory, mind and will, and asks only for love and grace. Today's word.
Your line: take, Lord, receive. Love shows itself more in deeds than in words. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1262.title: God in all things
1262.hook: Ignatian spirituality finds God in all things
1262.howItsDone: In the Ignatian tradition, people practice finding God in all things by paying attention to daily work, conversation and study as places of prayer, often looking back over the day in the examen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Suscipe, the prayer that hands everything back: freedom, memory, mind and will. Your line was take, Lord, receive.

A young Jesuit student sits at a desk with a grammar book open, and he is worried. He joined to pray, and now his days are full of verb endings and lecture notes. When does the real spiritual life begin? Ignatius's answer to students like him is not a longer hour in the chapel. Seek the presence of God in everything, he tells them: in conversation, in walking, in seeing, tasting, hearing, thinking, in all that they do. The grammar book is not in the way. Today's phrase is the short form of that answer.
screen: `A STUDENT AND A GRAMMAR BOOK.` → `WHEN DOES THE REAL PRAYER START?` → `SEEK GOD IN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: God in all things. Four words that can sound like a greeting card, but in the Ignatian tradition they carry weight. In the Contemplation to Attain Love, Ignatius asks the retreatant to consider how God dwells in creatures: giving being to the elements, life to the plants, feeling to the animals, understanding to people. Then a step further: God works and labors in all created things on our behalf. The world is not a stage set God left behind. It's a place where God is busy. Saint Paul says it to the crowd in Athens, in the Douay-Rheims: "For in him we live, and move, and are." In the guidance Ignatius wrote for Jesuits, he asks those in studies, who can't spend long hours in formal prayer, to find God in what's in front of them. A conversation can be a place of prayer. So can a walk, a meal, a page of hard reading. Two cautions keep this honest. It doesn't mean everything is God: Catholic teaching keeps the Creator and the creature distinct; God is present in things, not the same as them. And it doesn't mean everything that happens is good. Ignatius also wrote the rules for discernment, because some movements lead away from God. Finding God in all things is a habit of attention, not rose-colored glasses. It might mean noticing the steam off a cup of coffee, a coworker's patience, a child's question, and asking: where is God at work in this?
screen: `GOD DWELLS IN CREATURES.` · `GOD WORKS AND LABORS FOR US.` · `PRAYER IN A WALK, A MEAL, A PAGE.` · `NOT EVERYTHING IS GOD. NOT EVERYTHING IS GOOD.` · then, large: `IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE, AND ARE.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing in reach or in view, a cup, a window, your own hand, and look at it as if for the first time: its color, its weight, who made it. Then ask, without forcing an answer, how God might be at work in this one thing. If you pray, simply say thank you for it; if nothing comes, the looking itself is the practice.
God in all things. The Ignatian habit of looking for God's presence and work in ordinary life, in study and talk and meals, not only in church. Today's word.
Your line: all things. Even a washed dish or a red light counts. See you tomorrow.

1263.title: Contemplatives in action
1263.hook: early Jesuits described themselves as contemplatives in action
1263.howItsDone: Jesuits and people formed in Ignatian spirituality try to pray in the midst of work and travel, anchored by Mass, personal prayer and the daily examen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, God in all things: God present and at work in a cup, a page, a walk, yet never the same as them. Your line was all things.

You met the Society of Jesus back on day eight hundred forty-nine. Here's a puzzle its first members had to solve. Catholic religious life had a beautiful rhythm: monks and nuns, and later friars, gathering in choir through the day to chant the psalms together. The bell rang, and everyone came in from the fields. Ignatius and his companions wanted to be sent: to cities, to ports, to hospitals, to far countries, often alone. A bell in one chapel can't call a man who's on a ship. So how does a person pray when the job is to keep moving?
screen: `THE BELL CALLS THE CHOIR IN.` → `BUT WHAT IF YOU'RE ON A SHIP?` → `HOW DOES A TRAVELER PRAY?`

segments.voice: Their answer: contemplatives in action. The phrase is usually traced to Jerónimo Nadal, one of the early Jesuits, who traveled from house to house explaining the new order to its own members. Describing Ignatius, he said, in Latin, that he was contemplative even in action. Not contemplative first and active second, in two shifts. Both at once. So the new order made a choice that surprised people: the Jesuits did not gather in choir to chant the hours together the way monks and friars did. Each one still prayed, went to Mass and kept the daily examen, but the shape of the day was built for movement. That was no judgment on the monasteries. The Church keeps both, and the Carmelites, coming up soon on this path, will show the other shape. A different shape for a different job. What holds it together is yesterday's idea. If God is at work in all things, then the classroom, the sickroom and the road aren't interruptions to prayer. They're where prayer goes. Saint Paul packs it into three words in the Douay-Rheims: "Pray without ceasing." Nobody can kneel without ceasing, but a person can carry a quiet awareness of God through a busy day, the way you carry a song in your head. Some worry this becomes an excuse: I'm too busy to pray; my work is my prayer. The early Jesuits answered with the examen and the Exercises. Action stays prayer only if there's still a still point to return to. Motion and stillness, braided together.
screen: `NADAL: CONTEMPLATIVE EVEN IN ACTION.` · `NO CHOIR, BUILT FOR MOVEMENT.` · `THE ROAD IS WHERE PRAYER GOES.` · `STILL A STILL POINT TO RETURN TO.` · then, large: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: Choose one simple task right where you are, folding a cloth, wiping a table, straightening your desk, and do it slowly, with full attention. Let a short phrase ride along with each movement: if you pray, the name of Jesus, or Paul's pray without ceasing; if you don't, simply here, now.
Contemplatives in action. The early Jesuit ideal of praying in the middle of work and travel, not only apart from it, with the examen as the still point. Today's word.
Your line: prayer in motion. The still point keeps the motion honest. Until tomorrow.

1264.title: Care for the whole person
1264.hook: Jesuit schools care for the whole person
1264.howItsDone: Jesuit schools and universities describe cura personalis as attention to each student's intellectual, emotional and spiritual life, and the phrase often appears in their mission statements and advising programs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, contemplatives in action: no choir bell, a day built for being sent, and a still point to return to. Your line was prayer in motion.

A report card says a student is failing chemistry. One teacher sees a grade to fix. Another notices the student has been sleeping in the back row for weeks, asks a quiet question after class, and learns that someone at home is sick and the kid is working nights. Same student, same grade, two very different pictures of who is sitting in that chair. Jesuit schools have a two-word Latin phrase for the second kind of seeing, and some put it in their mission statements.
screen: `A FAILING GRADE.` → `A QUIET QUESTION AFTER CLASS.` → `WHO IS IN THAT CHAIR?`

segments.voice: Cura personalis. Cura means care; personalis, of the person. In English it usually comes out as care for the whole person. The idea is older than the slogan. In the guidance at the start of the Spiritual Exercises, Ignatius keeps telling the director to adapt. Give the Exercises according to the person's age, education and ability. Don't hand anyone more than they can carry. Notice whether they're in consolation or desolation, and respond to that person, not to a script. The retreat bends to fit the human being, not the other way round. Later Jesuits, tradition says, used cura personalis for the care superiors owed each member of the order, one by one. Jesuit schools took it up as a promise about students: we aren't only training a mind. We care about the body that's tired, the heart that's worried, the spirit that's searching. Saint Paul's blessing for the Thessalonians names all three, in the Douay-Rheims: "your whole spirit, and soul, and body." What makes it more than kindness? A Jesuit classroom is still a classroom, and the chemistry still matters. Cura personalis doesn't lower the bar; it asks who is trying to clear it, and what they're carrying. And it isn't only for schools. A nurse can practice it, a manager, a parent at a kitchen table. It's the difference between how are you, said on the way past, and how are you, said while you stop walking.
screen: `CURA: CARE. PERSONALIS: OF THE PERSON.` · `IGNATIUS: ADAPT TO EACH ONE.` · `MIND, BODY, HEART, SPIRIT.` · `IT DOESN'T LOWER THE BAR.` · then, large: `YOUR WHOLE SPIRIT, AND SOUL, AND BODY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you'll see or message soon, a coworker, a parent, a friend who's gone quiet, and picture them not as a role but as a whole person. What might their body be carrying, their mind, their heart? If you pray, hold that person before God for the length of this sit.
Cura personalis. Latin for care of the person: the Jesuit habit of attending to each one as a whole human being, mind, body and spirit. Today's word.
Your line: the whole person. The bar stays where it is, and the care comes with it. Same time tomorrow.

1265.title: The more
1265.hook: always the more, the greater good
1265.howItsDone: Jesuit schools and retreats speak of the magis as choosing what leads more to God's glory and the good of others; some students write AMDG, the Jesuit motto, at the top of their work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cura personalis: care for the whole person, mind, body and spirit, without lowering the bar. Your line was the whole person.

Four letters sit at the top of homework pages in some Jesuit schools, written before the student's name: A, M, D, G. They stand for a Latin motto of the Jesuits, ad maiorem Dei gloriam, for the greater glory of God. Notice the word in the middle. Not for the glory of God; for the greater glory. There's a comparison built into it, a reaching. Jesuits pulled that reaching out into a single Latin word you'll hear in their schools, retreats and homilies. It fits on a wristband, and it's easy to get badly wrong.
screen: `A. M. D. G.` → `FOR THE GREATER GLORY OF GOD.` → `NOT GREAT. GREATER.`

segments.voice: Magis. Latin for more. It shows up at the very end of the foundation in the Exercises, where Ignatius says we should desire and choose only what leads more to the end for which we are made. Not just a good choice: the choice that leads further toward God. Some readers hear that little comparison again and again in the Exercises. Here's the trap. Heard carelessly, magis sounds like more hours, more projects, more achievement, more pressure. A Jesuit motto for burnout. That's not what Ignatius means. The more is measured against one thing only: the love and service of God and neighbor. Sometimes the magis is doing more. Sometimes it's doing less, better. Sometimes it's resting, because a tired person loves badly. Sometimes it's saying no to a good thing to make room for a better one. That's why magis lives beside yesterday's cura personalis and the indifference from earlier in the Exercises. It's not a whip. It's a question asked with open hands: of the good options in front of me, which leads more toward love? Jesus describes his own purpose with a kind of more, in the Douay-Rheims of John's Gospel: "I am come that they may have life, and may have it more abundantly." Abundance, not exhaustion. In a plain week, magis might mean making the phone call instead of sending the text, reading the bedtime story slowly, spending five extra minutes to do a task well. Or closing the laptop, because the more for tonight is sleep.
screen: `MAGIS: MORE.` · `WHAT LEADS MORE TO OUR END.` · `NOT MORE HOURS. MORE LOVE.` · `SOMETIMES THE MORE IS LESS.` · then, large: `LIFE, MORE ABUNDANTLY.`

segments.voice: Think of something ordinary ahead of you, a meal, a message, a chore, and hold two versions side by side: the usual way, and a way with a little more love in it, more care or patience rather than more effort. Then ask honestly whether the more, this time, might be less. If you pray, ask God to show you which.
Magis. Latin for more: in the Ignatian sense, the choice that leads more toward God and neighbor, which isn't always the busier one. Today's word.

1266.title: The Salvadoran Jesuits (1989)
1266.hook: six Jesuits and two women killed at a university in San Salvador
1266.howItsDone: Catholics, and especially Jesuit schools and universities, remember the Salvadoran Jesuits and Elba and Celina Ramos with Masses, vigils and prayers for peace and justice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, magis: the more, measured by love and not by hours. Your line was magis.

A university campus in San Salvador, during a civil war. You met Oscar Romero earlier on this path; this is his country. The Jesuits who run the university live in a house on the grounds. They are professors: a philosopher, a psychologist, a sociologist, theologians, and an older priest who works with schools for the poor. A woman named Elba Ramos cooks and keeps house for them, and on this night she and her daughter Celina are sleeping there, in a room of the house. Before dawn, soldiers come through the gate. Today, stay with them quietly, and ask what kind of teaching gets a person killed.
screen: `A CAMPUS IN A CIVIL WAR.` → `PROFESSORS, A COOK, HER DAUGHTER.` → `SOLDIERS BEFORE DAWN.`

segments.voice: The Salvadoran Jesuits. That night, soldiers of the Salvadoran army killed six Jesuit priests at the Central American University, along with Elba and Celina Ramos. A United Nations truth commission later investigated and named the military as responsible. The rector was Ignacio Ellacuría, a philosopher. With him died Ignacio Martín-Baró, a psychologist; Segundo Montes, a sociologist; Amando López; Juan Ramón Moreno; and Joaquín López y López. Why them? They carried no weapons. They carried research, lectures and public arguments. Their university had spoken out about the poor and the suffering of ordinary people in the war, and it had pressed for a negotiated peace. For some in power, that teaching was dangerous. Here the last few days come home. Cura personalis, the whole person, stretched to a whole people. God in all things, including a country's poorest neighborhoods. The magis, asking what a university is for. These men had decided the answer included telling the truth out loud. And Elba and Celina are a reminder that the dead were not only the famous ones. In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Today, people come to the campus to pray where they died. The point is not drama. It's that teaching matters, and telling the truth in a classroom can cost something, in some places still.

1267.title: Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima (1945)
1267.hook: a Jesuit with medical training cares for the wounded after the atomic bomb
1267.carry: he turned the house into a hospital
1267.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the victims of war and for peace at Mass and in private prayer, and Arrupe's account of caring for the wounded at Hiroshima is often retold in Jesuit schools and retreats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salvadoran Jesuits, with Elba and Celina Ramos: a university that told the truth about the poor. Your line was killed for teaching.

A Spanish priest is in his room in a Jesuit house on the hills outside Hiroshima, where he trains young men who want to become Jesuits. Before joining the order he had studied medicine, though he hadn't practiced as a doctor in years. Then a blinding flash, a roar, and the windows blow in. He and the others climb the hill and look toward the city. It is burning. Before long, the wounded begin walking out of the smoke and up the road toward them. His name is Pedro Arrupe, and today, a damaged house and some half-forgotten training.
screen: `A JESUIT HOUSE ON THE HILLS.` → `A FLASH, THE WINDOWS BLOW IN.` → `THE WOUNDED WALK UP THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima. In his own later account, the house was cracked and battered but still standing. So he and the young Jesuits turned it into a hospital. The chapel, the rooms, the halls filled with people lying on mats. There was almost no medicine. He writes of doing what little he could with what was on hand, cleaning burns, trying to understand injuries no medical school had ever taught him. The young men became nurses overnight. They went into the ruins looking for survivors, and fed people from whatever food they could find. Arrupe didn't claim to have been a hero. What he describes is mostly helplessness, and staying anyway. The whole week gathers here. God in all things, even in a city in flames. Contemplatives in action: a house of prayer that became, without a vote, a house of nursing. Cura personalis, one burned person at a time. The magis, which in that moment simply meant: open the door wider. And after yesterday's teaching that cost something, here is care that costs something. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus names the people he will recognize at the end, and among them, in the Douay-Rheims: "sick, and you visited me." Arrupe later led the whole Society of Jesus. But the story people still tell is this house on the hill, and a man doing the next small thing because he was the one who was there.

segments.voice: Picture the road up the hill and the people walking out of the smoke, then think of one place at war right now: the people there whose names you'll never know, and those caring for them with almost nothing. Don't picture the worst; give them your breathing, one breath at a time. If you pray, pray for them and for peace; if you don't, let them stay in your thoughts a while.
